To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a new method for the optimisation and/or extension of PROSITE patterns is described.

(i) the procedure described in this manuscript allows one to build patterns which are more specific and/or sensitive than the original ones; (ii) in the cases where the procedure is able to improve the selectivity of the pattern, the structural information is used to identify residues which are functionally relevant and which can be used for the design of novel inhibitors.

a) a new procedure for improving the specificity and/or sensitivity for poorly-performing patterns was presented, b) the procedure was applied to eight different patterns and c) it was shown to be successful whenever the structurally conservd residues fall in the surface region.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the improvement of the quality of functional sequence patterns and with the identification of new residues involved in a specific protein function.
the identification of structural features that are important for the function of a protein, and with their use to improve pattern selectivities.
the improvement of the sensitivity and specificity of sequence patterns and with the identification of functionaly relevant structural information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the method described here is a valuable addition to the arsenal of tools available for the analysis of protein sequences and structures.
our procedure allows the identification of function-specific key residues and the construction of improved patterns, thus improving the quality of pattern databases and of pattern search tools.
our method can be used as a complementary approach to pattern construction and optimisation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a pattern can be improved by adding information derived from structural analysis, if such information is relevant for the function of the protein.
we have developed a new computational technique for the optimisation and the refinement of functional sequence patterns.
the method is able to improve the specificity and/or sensitivity for patterns which do not select all and only true positives.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of structural analysis and multiple sequence alignments can be used to improve the performance of patterns and, more generally, the identification of functional motifs in proteins.
the structural analysis of proteins sharing a common function can be a powerful tool to improve the quality of functional sequence patterns.

the use of structural information can be very useful for the improvement of the quality of patterns and that the structural information should be taken into consideration by pattern database curators.
